questions.stem: Why are the petals of an insect-pollinated flower large and brightly coloured?

options.text: To attract insects that carry pollen between flowers
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: To shield the ovules from rain
options.explanation: Petals are not the rain cover; sepals guard the bud.

options.text: To make the pollen fly further
options.explanation: Petal colour cannot launch pollen; a courier does the carrying.

options.text: To reflect heat away from the ovary
options.explanation: Temperature control is not a petal job here.

questions.stem: Which structure produces and releases the pollen grains?

options.text: The sepal
options.explanation: The sepal protects the unopened bud.

options.text: The anther
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The stigma
options.explanation: The stigma receives pollen; it never makes it.

options.text: The filament
options.explanation: The filament is the stalk that holds the anther up.

questions.stem: What keeps the anthers positioned so visiting insects cannot avoid them?

options.text: A ring of muscle around the ovary
options.explanation: Muscles belong to animal bodies, not flower stalks.

options.text: Sticky nectar gluing the anthers shut
options.explanation: Nectar rewards visitors; it does not anchor anthers.

options.text: Stiff filaments holding them inside the flower where bodies must brush past
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Long floppy stalks hanging outside the petals
options.explanation: Hanging outside is the wind-pollinated design, not the insect one.

questions.stem: Why is a sticky stigma an advantage for an insect-pollinated flower?

options.text: It dissolves the pollen to feed the style
options.explanation: The stigma collects grains; digestion happens later, after tube growth.

options.text: It stops insects from landing twice
options.explanation: Repeat visits are harmless; catching grains is the point.

options.text: It glues petals shut at night
options.explanation: Petal closure is not a stigma role.

options.text: It catches pollen grains off the bodies of brushing insects
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A bee enters a flower for nectar and leaves dusted with grains. Which sequence describes what it achieved?

options.text: It collected pollen while feeding and can deposit it on the next flower's stigma
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It fertilised the flower it fed on
options.explanation: Feeding alone does not complete fertilisation; delivery to another stigma is the pollination step.

options.text: It destroyed the anthers by feeding
options.explanation: Feeding on nectar does not strip the anthers.

options.text: It carried nectar instead of pollen
options.explanation: The cargo that matters is pollen on the body, not nectar.

questions.stem: State the flower structure whose job is to receive pollen grains.
questions.modelAnswer: The stigma is the sticky female surface that receives pollen grains.

questions.stem: Name the two flower parts that produce scent and nectar rewards for insect visitors.
questions.modelAnswer: Scent plus nectar exist to draw insect visitors in and reward them for arriving.

questions.stem: Explain why an insect-pollinated flower wastes no effort on tiny, dull petals.
questions.modelAnswer: Dull small petals would fail the flower's only recruitment tool, since insects find these flowers by sight, so large bright petals are what attract the couriers.

questions.stem: A gardener breeds a variety with almost no scent. Predict the effect on insect visits and explain your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Visits should drop, since scent and nectar exist to draw insects in, so a scentless variety loses its main long-range signal.

questions.stem: Why do wind-pollinated flowers make no scent or nectar?

options.text: Because nectar dries out the anthers
options.explanation: Nectar does not drain the anthers.

options.text: Because no couriers need rewarding, so producing them would waste energy
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because scent would poison the pollen
options.explanation: Scent does not chemically harm pollen.

options.text: Because wind destroys scent molecules
options.explanation: The wind scatters smells; it does not make them pointless.

questions.stem: Which feature lets a wind-pollinated flower shed its grains into the moving air most easily?

options.text: Sticky pollen clumped on stiff stalks
options.explanation: Stickiness suits insect carriage, not wind release.

options.text: A feathery stigma inside the ovary
options.explanation: The stigma is female and sits outside, not in the ovary.

options.text: Anthers hanging outside the flower on long filaments
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Anthers locked deep inside the petals
options.explanation: Deep placement would shield grains from the airflow.

questions.stem: What is the job of a feathery stigma in a wind-pollinated flower?

options.text: To produce nectar for insects
options.explanation: Feathery stigmas do not reward couriers.

options.text: To wrap the seeds after fertilisation
options.explanation: Fruit, not stigma, wraps seeds.

options.text: To push the pollen tube down the style
options.explanation: The tube grows by itself; the stigma just receives grains.

options.text: To present a wide surface that catches airborne pollen grains
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: A wind-pollinated flower's petals are small and often green or brown. What does this contrast with?

options.text: The large, brightly coloured petals of insect-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The sticky stigmas of insect-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: The contrast asked for is petal colour and size.

options.text: The long filaments of insect-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: Filament length is an anther feature, not a petal one.

options.text: The nectar of wind-pollinated flowers
options.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers make no nectar at all.

questions.stem: Wind pollination is a numbers game. Why can these flowers afford to release so many grains that never land on a stigma?

options.text: Grains that miss germinate on leaves
options.explanation: Missed grains are simply lost.

options.text: Pollen is cheap to produce in bulk, and exposure beats attraction when no courier is hired
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Every grain is guided to a stigma by scent
options.explanation: Scent is absent in wind-pollinated flowers.

options.text: The wind carries each grain precisely
options.explanation: Airflow is random; most grains miss.

questions.stem: State where the anthers of a wind-pollinated flower hang and why.
questions.modelAnswer: The anthers hang outside the flower on long filaments so the wind can blow the pollen away.

questions.stem: Describe the petals of a wind-pollinated flower.
questions.modelAnswer: The petals keep a small, dull look, commonly green or brown.

questions.stem: Explain why hanging both anthers and stigmas outside the flower suits wind pollination.
questions.modelAnswer: Hanging outside puts the anthers directly in the airflow that carries grains away and puts the feathery stigmas in the path of grains drifting from other flowers.

questions.stem: A grass flower growing in a sheltered, still courtyard sets few seeds. Suggest why, using the wind-pollination adaptation you have learned.
questions.modelAnswer: With little moving air, the exposed anthers release pollen that never drifts far, so few grains reach the feathery stigmas of neighbouring flowers.
